title: Who else feels games are less valuable now?
author: TheGamingSpringbok
selftext:
I feel as time progresses games are genuinely becoming less valuable (financially at least for devs to make money)

Games are becoming cheaper to make because of AI.

And we also see games being mass produced because of it. 

I got a kid to playtest my indie game (Twilight Tavern) recently and they had a lot of fun with it to my surprise, literally jump and down lmao. 

Anyways the kid wanted to show me games they liked on their phone and to my surprise they showed me a bunch of website and browser based games that are clearly AI made. 

And these games are free, copycats, etc. 

There was this game almost identical to Minecraft and I asked the kid "wouldn't you prefer playing Minecraft" in which she responded "no i find this more fun". 

Even as I browse X, Reddit and other platforms there's tons of games now. As a game dev myself it is especially brutal to stand out. 

Im feeling there's more far more value in standing out like a popularity contest then there has ever been. Making games are now so much smoother, easier, the skills to make one feel less valuable to me at least. 

Anyone else feel this way or have a different perspective on this?

comments.author: MuhEry22
comments.body: I agree. If, in the near future, we reach a point where we can create the exact same game just by using a few prompts—instead of buying it—then why would we bother buying it at all? Or, whenever you come up with a game concept, you’ll likely find that it has already been made. There is such an overwhelming volume of content being produced that creating something truly new has become impossible. Even if you do manage to release a game based on a great idea, clones of it will appear almost instantly. It’s a worrying situation.

replies.author: TheGamingSpringbok
replies.body: Yea now that i think about it , my game being vreated by just a few prompts definetly is worrying.

replies.author: UnimagineDragons
replies.body:
There's lots of examples of why this won't be the case in real life. If one thing is for certain, humans love to take a concept and apply "infinity" to it but it is always a quick ride to incorrect. World wars would mean war forever, internet means no one works ever, globalism means mass authoritarianism, airplanes mean the end of ground transportation, one pandemic means the end of the world etc. 

For the topic at hand, one thing will always be attractive and that's real live people. If there are 20 counterstrike clones out there, the one that wins is the one that people meet up in and actually play. There will always be a way to differentiate your game and keeping the attention of people will be more important than simply coding and releasing.

The software jobs that were focused on building will now have to be re-tooled into "player attraction and retention" positions and the strategy to attract paying customers will be the differentiator vs. the software itself.

We will always find some software better, cooler, faster, more popular etc. and word of mouth and "trendy" things will always guide the masses

replies.author: couldgiveaflyingfck
replies.body: I honestly don't care how a game was made either, as long as it's good. If it's fun, engaging, and captures my attention - if it's one of those games that I want to play the very first thing when I wake up - that is exactly what I'm looking for. To be honest, I feel the same way about movies. I would sit here and watch an AI-generated vintage Bruce Lee movie in an absolute heartbeat. As long as it was done well and captured the emotion, the action was crazy, and the story was good, I'm in. AI can do that. I do not care about AI at all. I love it no matter what.

comments.author: couldgiveaflyingfck
comments.body: Of course they're less valuable. I'm going to tell you something else: they're going to continue to get less valuable. The reason is simple. The barrier to entry has been knocked down. Anybody can come in here with a Claude Ultra account and, within a few weeks or a few months, develop an extremely polished commercial game. Of course, the quality will depend on their skill set—how much time they are willing to invest in researching how to be a developer, how games are actually made, and the blueprints for creating a great game. It is going to get crazy. A lot of people and companies are going to make a lot less money. It is going to put a tremendous amount of pressure on everybody, especially the big companies. I've already expressed my belief on this. My logic is that Microsoft will probably end up selling its games division since it has already performed poorly. Now they have all this pressure from what feels like a million new developers. I don't know exactly where I'm getting that number from, but there are a lot of new AI game developers out there with Claude Ultra accounts, and that is going to put massive pressure on the industry. By this time next year, for every game that is out there, you are going to see a hundred copies of it. I am not talking about cloning. Cloning is when you say, "Hey, make Super Mario Brothers for me." That is not what I mean. I am talking about original ideas that use the same game mechanics but just do the job better.

replies.author: Jacmac_
replies.body: Seriously. It's going to get to the point a few decades from now that buying a game won't really be necessary since AI will be capable of generating it on the fly like the Star Trek Holodeck. The people making the money will shift from game developers to the AI developers.

What do you mean we need a sound for every single tiny miniscule thing. Every little interaction. Every menu blip and walking surface. I can see why GTA 6 cost a bajillion dollars and 1000 devs.

comments.author: Jacmac_
comments.body:
This is natural. Henry Ford introduced mass production of automobiles and dumped vehicles on the market faster than hand made vehicles. Johannes Gutenberg introduced the printing press, so books were no longer books were copied by hand. Michael Owens created the automatic bottle-making machine, where before glass bottles had been blown by hand. It goes on and on.

This is just another iteration of technology that will put a lot of hand made, labor intensive processes out to pasture. As far as the artists suffering, there will still be a place for artists; but lets face it, very very few are Picaso's. 99% of the stuff programmed and created by a solo artist completely by hand are paintings hanging on the wall at the local restaurant waiting to be bought before some kid flips their pancakes and syrup on them.
